chunks: "A ground plane is a solid layer that all ground connections drop into with a via. Ground traces are routed connections: a daisy chain, a star or a grid.

One ounce copper is about half a milliohm per square, so a plane between two points is under a milliohm, while a 100 millimetre, quarter-millimetre ground trace is 190 milliohms and around 140 nanohenries, about 90 ohms at 100 megahertz.

The plane also gives each signal a return path right underneath it, so loops are small; with traces the return is wherever you routed it, usually far from the signal, so loops are big, which means more radiation and pickup.
And with a plane there's no shared-impedance coupling to speak of, while a daisy chain adds up every upstream load's current in the downstream segments.
The costs of the plane are layers and money, plus capacitance and the other things we covered.

Traces make sense on one or two-layer boards where a plane isn't affordable, and where you want a deliberately separated ground, like a star point for a shunt measurement or for separating a motor return.
Even then I use wide traces or a ground pour, a grid if I can, and keep the signal and its return together. So: plane by default, traces when the cost or the topology demands it."
